newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. adds 210,000 new jobs in Oct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. adds 210,000 new jobs in Oct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department said the economy created 210,000 new jobs in October compared to a revised reduction of 35,000 jobs in September.
The unemployment rate stood at 5.2 percent, unchanged from September. Experts had expected 212,000 new jobs in the month and a jobless rate of 5.2 percent.
AUDREY FREEDMAN, PRESIDENT, AUDREY FREEDMAN AND ASSOCIATES INC: "These figures are showing a steady economy, more growth than I certainly expected."
Freedman, speaking on Reuters Financial Television, added: "All the indicators should tell the (Federal Reserve) to leave well enough alone."

EVELINA TAINER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, INDOSUEZ CARR FUTURES: "It's a perfect number. The Fed's going to love it. It puts the three-month average at 152,000, which means we're growing at a nice pace but not too slow, not too fast. It does signal that it is possible we could go a little bit lower on the jobless rate and not necessarily cause inflationary pressures, especially with hourly earnings unchanged for the month."

HUGH JOHNSON, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER, FIRST ALBANY CORP: "The increase in jobs of 210,000 as well as the upward revision to September of 5,000 is slightly bad news, but the big news if there's a surprise in the number is average hourly earnings which stayed the same.

"So, despite the fact the unemployment rate is 5.2 percent and labor market conditions are still arguably tight, there's not much upward pressure on wages, and that is likely to be a relief to the bond market and the Federal Reserve."

ASTRID ADOLFSON, FIRST VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH: "It was a good report, which was in line with consenseus. It shows that payrolls and the economy are growing moderately. The most important thing is that average hourly earnings were flat, which shows that wage pressure are abating. However, the numbers were not weak enough for the Federal Reserve to ease."
DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "Markets are celebrating that average hourly earnings were flat after last month's increase."

WALDO BEST, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BZW GOVERNMENT SECURITIES INC: "The numbers are going to cause some people to rethink the third-quarter GDP numbers, thinking that maybe there's going to be an upward revision to that number showing a little more strength in the third quarter.

"In terms of what we're looking at for September, it's pretty much what was expected -- a moderate report. The employment rate didn't move and we saw some weakeness in the manufacturing area as far as earnings and overtime, largely due to some effects of the General Motors' strike."

Best continued: "When you look at the report net-net, it's not setting off any signals that there's an inflation problem based on these numbers, and it's saying the economy really isn't in any major trouble.

"Most of the weakness here is strike-related, so it's a good number in terms of the economy, a number that the bond number can live with and maybe rally on, and it's a good number for Bill Clinton because it says that although the economy's not taking off, it's not headed toward a recession either," he added.
CAROL STONE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA SECURITIES
INTERNATIONAL INC: "The total is pretty much of a non-event for a change, and so is the unemployment rate.

"The positive factor here is earnings stabilized after having been up in the previous couple of months, and they stabilized in the face of forecasts calling for continued increases, partly because of the minimum wage taking effect at the beginning of the month "This plays right into the Fed's steady scenario."

KEN BERCUSON, HEAD OF ECONOMIC RESEARCH, SBC WARBURG: "The numbers are surprising, particularly on wages. One would have certainly expected to see more signs of wage pressures. But I think that will pick up (again) later in the quarter.
He noted that the diffusion index between firms that are hiring and those decreasing labor jumped in October.
"The demand for labor is pretty strong. The labor market is still very, very tight, and we're not going to see flat wages continue," he added. -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660
